purpose: How an operator selling home service contracts reads the actual contract at component level, converts its exclusions, dollar limits, waiting period and pre-existing-condition clause into decision mechanisms, surfaces every one of them to the buyer before money changes hands, matches plan tier to the realistic failure risk of the specific home including the recommendation not to buy, and leaves behind a documented record that protects the client and the seller equally.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors

the operator is a seller or sales agency for home service contracts issued by a third-party obligor, not the obligor, not the administrator, not the servicing contractor, and not a licensed insurance adjuster

home service contracts are regulated products whose registration, licensing, required disclosures, permitted wording, cancellation and refund rights and record-keeping duties differ by state and change over time, so every regulatory point here is an obligation class whose current specifics must be verified in the operating jurisdiction before selling

the contract document that will be issued to the buyer, in the edition and state form that applies to the sale, is available to the seller before the sale and is the sole authority on coverage; brochures, training decks, comparison charts and remembered plan facts are not
coverage determinations at claim time belong to the obligor on the evidence the servicing technician produces; nothing the seller says, writes or believes changes that outcome

no dollar figure of any kind is asserted here: caps, fees, prices, repair costs and commissions are described only as mechanisms that produce a number, and the real numbers are read off this contract and off the client's own local quotes
the work in this knowledge base ends when the sale closes and the closing packet is handed over; everything that happens afterward is servicing, claims guidance and renewal
exclusions: how the product itself is constructed and who stands behind it - obligor and administrator roles, term structure, how caps are engineered into the plan design, reimbursement-insurance backing, and the choice of which provider to represent; that is the service-contract products and distribution channels knowledge base this one stands on

distribution channels and their economics - realtor and closing-table placement, direct-to-homeowner marketing, property-manager and trade-partner arrangements, per-channel compensation structure and the compliance class attached to each channel; those belong to the products and distribution knowledge base

what happens after the sale - guiding a client through an open claim, arguing a denial, renewal pricing and renewal conversations, retention measurement, reputation and review management, and the decision to advise a client that a plan is no longer worth renewing; that is the renewals, claims experience and reputation knowledge base this one hands off to at the closing packet

claim adjudication itself: diagnosing a failure, deciding whether a specific breakdown is covered, authorizing or denying repair, setting repair-versus-replace, and any appeal of an obligor decision, all of which belong to the obligor, its administrator and the servicing contractor

personalized legal, insurance, tax or financial advice to any individual buyer; this is operator education about how a contract is read, explained, matched and documented, and any recommendation to a real client is valid only when it rests on that client own home, contract edition and jurisdiction

state-specific specifics of provider registration, seller licensing, required contract wording and notices, permitted use of the word insurance, statutory free-look and refund mechanics, transfer rules and record-retention periods, all of which appear here only as obligation classes to verify in the operating jurisdiction

invented figures of any kind: contract prices, per-visit fees, coverage caps, repair or replacement costs, failure rates, commission percentages and renewal values are expressed as the mechanism that produces them and how to verify each on the specific deal, never as a stated number

any promise, projection or implication that a particular failure will be covered, that a claim will be approved, that a contractor will arrive within a stated time, or that the plan will save the client money

technical trade knowledge: diagnosing why a compressor failed, estimating a repair, sizing equipment or performing any of the maintenance the contract requires, all of which belong to licensed trades rather than to the seller

selection and administration of the seller own tools - customer records systems, e-signature platforms, call recording and document storage - which are used here according to provider and jurisdictional rules but whose implementation is out of scope

competency_questions.question: What exactly is the agent promising when they sell a home service contract, what belongs to the obligor, and how is that boundary stated to a buyer who wants to hear that everything is handled?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SELLER_PROMISE_BOUNDARY states what the seller sells and what the obligor decides, and COVERAGE_QUESTION_HANDLING supplies the answer form that keeps every spoken answer inside that boundary

competency_questions.question: Which regulatory obligation classes govern what must be disclosed and delivered to a buyer of a service contract, and how does an operator work when the specifics differ by state?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: JURISDICTION_DISCLOSURE_OBLIGATIONS names the obligation classes and the verify-in-jurisdiction discipline, and SAMPLE_CONTRACT_DELIVERY shows how the right state edition reaches the buyer before purchase

competency_questions.question: In what order does the coverage conversation run so that exclusions, caps, the waiting period and the per-visit fee are surfaced before money changes hands rather than discovered at the first claim?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DISCLOSURE_FIRST_STANDARD fixes the order and the before-payment rule, and EXPECTATION_SETTING_PREVIEW adds the walkthrough of what filing a claim will actually feel like

competency_questions.question: How is the contract document itself read before anyone tries to explain it, and why does the definitions section decide more claims than the covered-items list?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CONTRACT_ANATOMY_READ gives the fixed reading order, names the edition-and-state discipline, and explains why contract-specific definitions of ordinary words control outcomes

competency_questions.question: A client asks whether their air conditioner is covered; what is the truthful answer and what has to exist before the seller can give it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: COVERED_COMPONENT_MAP supplies the component-level lookup including which parts of the system are listed, and COVERAGE_QUESTION_HANDLING supplies the three-part answer form ending in who decides at claim time

competency_questions.question: What are the recurring families of exclusions in this product class, and by what mechanism will each one actually be applied when a technician stands in front of a broken unit?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: EXCLUSION_TAXONOMY names the families and the evidence mechanism behind each, and MAINTENANCE_PROOF_BURDEN explains the maintenance family and the record habit that answers it

competency_questions.question: How do the contract dollar limits and the per-visit fee decide whether this plan is worth buying for this home, and which tier follows from that?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CAPS_AND_LIMITS_MECHANICS puts the applicable limit beside a locally sourced replacement cost and adds the fee and cash-in-lieu mechanisms, and PLAN_TIER_FIT applies the upgrade test to the specific home

competency_questions.question: When does coverage actually start on this contract, and how is the first-claim window explained to a buyer who has a problem right now?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: WAITING_PERIOD_AND_EFFECTIVE_DATE derives the start date and waiting-period end from the contract itself, names the real-estate-transaction difference as a contract term, and states what happens when a closing slips

competency_questions.question: How is the pre-existing-condition clause explained honestly, and what does the seller do when the client describes a system that is already failing?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRE_EXISTING_CONDITION_CLAUSE presents the clause as a known-or-detectable evidence test, and CLIENT_CONDITION_INTAKE records the client own account of system condition in their words and dates it

competency_questions.question: How is the realistic failure-risk profile of a specific home built and presented without sliding into fear-selling or invented numbers?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HOME_RISK_PROFILE builds the profile from observable inputs expressed as bands and mechanisms, and PLAN_COMPARISON_WITHOUT_FEAR states the normalized comparison axes and the prohibition on catastrophe framing and unsourced figures

competency_questions.question: Under what conditions should the seller tell a prospect not to buy this plan at all, and what does that conversation leave behind?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DECLINE_TO_SELL_PATH lists the triggers for a no-sale recommendation and names the written artifact and alternative advice the client leaves with

competency_questions.question: What must exist in the file after the sale so that both the client account and the seller account of what was disclosed survive a dispute a year later?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DISCLOSURE_EVIDENCE_FILE enumerates the contemporaneous artifacts and the same-day writing rule, and CLOSING_PACKET_HANDOFF states what the client physically leaves with and the gate that must pass first

competency_questions.question: How does the conversation change for a buyer who is elderly, under closing-day pressure, or reading a contract written in their second language?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: VULNERABLE_BUYER_CARE gives the pacing, third-party and stop-the-sale protocol, and PLAIN_LANGUAGE_TRANSLATION gives the rule that a simplified sentence may never widen the promise

glossary.definition: The product being sold: a written agreement under which a named obligor arranges and pays for repair or replacement of specific listed home systems and appliances that break down during the term, subject to stated exclusions, dollar limits, conditions and a per-visit fee. Whether it is regulated as insurance, as a service contract under a consumer-protection statute, or under a separate registration regime depends on the state and must be verified locally.

The party named in the contract that is financially responsible for performing it and that makes the coverage determination on each claim. The seller is not the obligor; identifying the obligor in the document and telling the buyer who it is is part of the disclosure conversation.

The entity that runs the claim process day to day - takes the call, assigns a contractor from its network, collects the diagnosis and applies the contract to it. Buyers experience the administrator as the plan, which is why the seller previews how that process works before the sale.

A system or appliance named in the covered-items schedule. Coverage is decided at component level inside that item, so the operational unit is not the appliance name but the list of parts the contract includes and the parts it silently leaves out.

The mechanism that caps what the obligor will pay - per covered item per term, per system or trade, as an aggregate across the whole term, or as a sub-limit on a specific component. Its practical meaning is only visible when placed beside what the repair costs in that local market.

The amount the contract requires the homeowner to pay on each dispatch, due whether or not the visit results in covered work, and sometimes due again when a second trade is dispatched for the same problem. It is read off the contract, never quoted from memory.

The interval stated in the contract between purchase or effective date and the first date a claim can be made, which exists to stop a plan being bought as a repair order. Its length and how it interacts with a real-estate closing are contract terms that vary by plan and edition.

A failure that existed before coverage began, applied at claim time as an evidence test with two halves: whether the buyer knew of it, and whether it would have been detectable by visual inspection or simple mechanical test. Unknown does not rescue a condition a walkthrough would have shown.

The mechanism by which an obligor may settle a covered claim with a payment rather than performing the repair, generally calculated on what the work would cost the obligor through its own network rather than the retail price the homeowner would pay a contractor of their choice.

The period after purchase in which a buyer may cancel and receive a refund calculated by a stated method, and the later cancellation terms that apply after it. Whether such a window is mandatory, how long it runs and how the refund is computed are jurisdiction-dependent obligation classes to verify locally.

nodes.definition: The first act of competence in this business is naming, out loud and in the file, what is actually being sold: a specific written contract with a list of covered components, a set of exclusions, stated dollar limits and stated claim conditions - not a promise that the home will be taken care of. The obligor named in the contract decides claims on the evidence a technician produces; the administrator assigns the contractor; the seller explains the document, matches it to the home and records the explanation, and has no authority to approve, deny or reverse anything. That boundary is stated to the buyer before the first coverage question is answered, because every reputational disaster in this vertical starts with a homeowner who believed the person who sold the plan had personally promised the outcome. The boundary also fixes the seller vocabulary: descriptions of what the document says, mechanisms for how a determination will be made, and the honest sentence that the obligor decides that at claim time - never a guarantee, never a personalized legal or insurance opinion, and never the word insurance where the contract and the jurisdiction do not support it.

included: the sentence that separates explaining a contract from guaranteeing a result
who decides claims and who does not, stated to the buyer before coverage is discussed
the vocabulary limits that keep spoken answers inside the document
excluded: which provider or obligor the operator chooses to represent and why
conduct during an open claim or a denial, which belongs to the claims-experience knowledge base
the obligor internal coverage determination process

pros.claim: Naming the boundary before the pitch converts a future denial from a betrayal into a remembered conversation
pros.example: a homeowner whose compressor claim is denied for a non-covered secondary cause recalls being told at sale that the obligor decides on the technician diagnosis, and calls the seller for help rather than filing a complaint about them

pros.claim: It keeps the seller inside the one role they can actually perform, which is the only role they can be judged on
pros.example: an agent who promised nothing about outcomes can still be measured on whether the exclusions were explained, and that is a standard they can meet on every sale

cons.claim: Stating the limits of your own authority weakens the emotional pitch and some prospects hear it as hedging
cons.example: a buyer at a closing table who wanted to hear that it is all handled reads the boundary statement as a lack of confidence in the product

cons.claim: The boundary is easy to state once and then abandon under a direct question
cons.example: an agent who opened with the obligor decides, and forty minutes later answers a specific question with do not worry, they will take care of it

failure_modes: sliding into we will take care of you language that a buyer reasonably hears as a personal guarantee
answering a coverage question as though the seller made the determination
describing a service contract as insurance in a jurisdiction or a document that does not support the word
letting a third party at the table make the promise while the seller stays silent
acceptance_tests: the buyer can restate in their own words that the obligor decides claims and the seller explains and documents the contract
the file carries a dated note that the promise boundary was stated before any coverage question was answered
no written or recorded sentence from the seller guarantees a claim outcome or a service timeline
revisit_triggers: the obligor or administrator behind the plan changes and the claim decision path changes with it
a complaint or chargeback alleges the seller promised an outcome
the operator begins selling in a jurisdiction with different rules on how the product may be described

base.update_signal: a complaint, chargeback or regulator inquiry alleging that the seller promised a claim outcome, or a change in the obligor behind the plans being sold

nodes.definition: Home service contracts are regulated products, and the classes of rule that bite in this subdomain are the ones governing what must be disclosed and delivered to the buyer: whether the contract itself must be given before or at sale, what identification of the provider and obligor and any reimbursement-insurance backing must appear in it, whether the buyer has a statutory cancellation or free-look right and how a refund is calculated, what wording is restricted or prohibited when describing the product, what a seller may state about who stands behind the plan, and what records of the transaction must be retained and for how long. Each of these is an obligation class rather than a memorized fact: which agency regulates the product, whether it sits under an insurance code or a consumer-protection statute, and the specifics of every item above vary by state and change. The competent operator keeps a per-state checklist of which classes apply, sources it from the current statute and the provider compliance materials, and verifies current rules in the operating jurisdiction before selling - treating anything remembered from a neighbouring state as a hypothesis to confirm, never as a rule.

included: the classes of disclosure, delivery, cancellation-right and record-keeping obligation attached to selling a service contract
the discipline of verifying current specifics in the operating jurisdiction before each sale
restrictions on how the product may be described to a buyer
excluded: provider registration and seller licensing mechanics, and the compliance class attached to each distribution channel, which belong to the products and distribution knowledge base
any assertion of what a specific state currently requires
legal advice on statutory interpretation, which belongs to counsel

pros.claim: A per-state checklist of obligation classes makes compliance a repeatable pre-sale step instead of a memory test
pros.example: before the first sale in a new state the operator confirms whether a cancellation window is mandatory and how the refund is computed, rather than assuming the practice used next door

pros.claim: Naming obligations as classes rather than facts keeps the knowledge from silently expiring
pros.example: a rule change on required contract disclosures updates one checklist line instead of invalidating a whole trained script

cons.claim: Verification takes real time before revenue in every new jurisdiction and cannot be delegated to a script
cons.example: an operator expanding across a state line has to re-source the current rules before selling a single contract there

cons.claim: Checklists tempt operators into treating compliance as complete when a class was simply never noticed
cons.example: a checklist with no line for record retention passes cleanly while the retention duty goes unmet

failure_modes: carrying a practice learned in one state into another as though it were the rule
relying on a provider marketing summary rather than the current statute or compliance materials
describing the product with restricted wording because a competitor does
letting the checklist go stale after a rule change
acceptance_tests: a current per-state checklist exists naming each applicable obligation class and where its specifics were sourced
every regulatory statement made to a buyer is traceable to that checklist rather than to memory
the checklist carries a date and a review cadence
revisit_triggers: the operator begins selling into a new state or a new plan family
the provider issues updated compliance materials or a new contract form
a rule change, bulletin or enforcement action touches service-contract disclosure or cancellation rights

base.update_signal: a statutory or regulatory change, a provider compliance bulletin, or entry into a state not already on the checklist

nodes.definition: The operating rule of the whole subdomain: the buyer sees and hears the exclusions, the dollar limits, the waiting period, the per-visit fee and the claim conditions before money changes hands or a signature is taken - not in a follow-up email, not in a link at the bottom of a receipt, and not as fine print handed across the table at the close. Concretely the conversation runs in a fixed order - what is covered at component level, what is excluded and by what mechanism, what the limits are against real local repair cost, when coverage starts, what the client pays per visit, and who decides at claim time - and the exclusions get at least as much airtime as the covered-items list. Burying them is this vertical core ethical failure and its most reliable generator of chargebacks, complaints and dead referral sources; one sale that survives full disclosure is worth several that do not, because only the first kind renews. The standard is testable rather than aspirational: the file has to show what was disclosed, when, in what form, and what the buyer said back.

included: the before-payment rule and the fixed order of the coverage conversation
the airtime parity between the covered-items list and the exclusions
the requirement that disclosure leave evidence behind
excluded: the substance of individual exclusions and limits, which the reading nodes supply
renewal-time disclosure conversations, which belong to the renewals knowledge base
channel-specific marketing disclosures, which belong to the distribution knowledge base

pros.claim: Disclosure before payment removes the single most common cause of a cancelled contract in the first weeks
pros.example: a buyer who learns about the waiting period at sale does not call to cancel in anger when a claim filed in week one is refused

pros.claim: It converts the sale into a decision the buyer owns, which is what makes them a renewer and a referrer
pros.example: a homeowner who chose the plan knowing ductwork was excluded treats a ductwork quote as expected rather than as a betrayal

cons.claim: Full disclosure measurably reduces close rate on impulse and pressure-driven sales
cons.example: a closing-table prospect who would have signed on a two-minute summary declines once the exclusion families are laid out

cons.claim: The conversation takes time that compressed channels have not budgeted for
cons.example: a walkthrough scheduled around a real-estate closing calendar that allots minutes rather than a call

failure_modes: reciting exclusions so fast or so late that disclosure is technically true and practically absent
sending the contract after payment and calling that disclosure
letting a co-present third party summarize the plan generously while the seller does not correct it
disclosing only the exclusions that seem unlikely to matter for this home
acceptance_tests: no payment or signature is taken on a file where the exclusions, limits, waiting period and fee were not walked through first
the file shows the disclosure date and form and precedes the payment date
the buyer restated at least the limits that bind on their own most expensive realistic failure
revisit_triggers: cancellations or complaints cluster on a term the buyer says was never mentioned
the contract edition changes what must be surfaced
a channel begins compressing the sale below the time the walkthrough needs

base.update_signal: a pattern of early cancellations or complaints naming a term the buyer says was not disclosed, or a contract edition that adds a term needing disclosure

nodes.definition: Some buyers cannot absorb a contract walkthrough at ordinary speed, and this product is disproportionately sold to them: older homeowners on fixed incomes taking an inbound call, first-time buyers signing a stack of documents on closing day, people reading the contract in a second language, heirs managing a house they have never lived in, and anyone in the middle of a household emergency. The protocol is concrete. Slow the pace and stop selling the moment confusion appears; never close on the same contact when the buyer cannot restate the three limits that matter for their home; invite a trusted family member, friend or adviser onto the call or into the room and welcome their questions; leave the document and the time to read it; state the cancellation or free-look right as it exists in their jurisdiction rather than hoping they never find it; refuse urgency framing, price-expires framing and catastrophe stories entirely; and record the accommodation in the file. Where the buyer cannot follow the material at all, the sale does not happen. Treating this as a first-class rule rather than a courtesy is what separates a durable book from a complaint file.

included: signals that a buyer needs a slower or supported process
the pacing, third-party-present and stop-the-sale rules
the ban on urgency and fear framing with at-risk buyers
excluded: any assessment of legal capacity, which is not the seller to make
the substance of the coverage explanation itself
renewal-time care for an ageing client, which belongs to the renewals knowledge base

pros.claim: A supported buyer makes a decision that holds, which protects the operator from the complaints that follow pressure sales
pros.example: an adult daughter joining the call asks the ductwork question her father would not have thought of, and the contract that results is never disputed

pros.claim: Explicit stop rules give the seller permission to walk away from the sale most likely to become a regulatory problem
pros.example: an inbound caller who cannot restate the waiting period after two attempts is thanked and sent the document rather than closed

cons.claim: The protocol costs the sales that a fast close would have captured, and those losses are visible while the avoided complaints are not
cons.example: a same-day close deferred to a second call that the prospect never takes

cons.claim: Vulnerability signals are read imperfectly and can shade into condescension
cons.example: an entirely capable older homeowner treated as fragile and slowed down when they wanted a direct answer

failure_modes: using urgency or scarcity framing on a buyer who is already anxious
closing on the same contact despite obvious confusion because the objection sounded soft
improvising a translation the seller cannot verify rather than sourcing the provider translated material or an interpreter
leaving the accommodation undocumented so the care taken is invisible later
acceptance_tests: no sale closes on a contact where the buyer could not restate the waiting period, the fee and the exclusion that most affects their home
where a vulnerability signal appeared, the file records the accommodation made and whether a third party was present
no recorded or written material used with these buyers contains urgency, scarcity or catastrophe framing
revisit_triggers: a complaint arrives from a family member rather than the buyer
a channel starts producing a higher share of at-risk buyers, such as an inbound line reaching mostly retirees
the jurisdiction adds or changes protections for older or vulnerable consumers

base.update_signal: a complaint raised by a relative or adviser on a buyer behalf, or a change in consumer-protection rules covering older buyers

nodes.definition: Read the document the buyer will actually receive, cover to cover, in a fixed order, before ever trying to explain it. Definitions first, because the contract redefines ordinary words and those redefinitions decide claims - what counts as a malfunction, what normal wear and tear means, what accessible means, what belongs to a system rather than to the structure. Then the covered-items schedule, then exclusions and limitations, then the schedule of dollar limits and fees, then the conditions block holding the waiting period, effective date, transfer on sale of the home, cancellation and refund method and any dispute-resolution or arbitration clause, and finally the identification of obligor and administrator. Record the edition or form identifier and the state it belongs to, because a plan sold under one form is a different product from the same plan sold under another. The output is a marked-up working copy plus a one-page teaching summary, rebuilt whenever the form changes. Selling from a brochure, a training deck or memory is the root cause of nearly every unintentional misrepresentation in this business.

included: the reading order and why definitions come first
capture of edition, form identifier and applicable state
the marked-up working copy and one-page teaching summary as artifacts
excluded: how the product was designed and priced by the provider, which belongs to the products knowledge base
legal interpretation of an ambiguous clause, which goes to counsel or to the provider in writing
explaining the contract to the buyer, which is the translation and disclosure work

pros.claim: Reading definitions first prevents the confident wrong answer that a covered-items list alone invites
pros.example: learning that access is defined narrowly explains in advance why a slab-embedded pipe repair will be treated differently from an under-sink one

pros.claim: An edition-stamped working copy makes every later statement traceable to a document rather than to memory
pros.example: a coverage claim made in a proposal can be pointed at a section number in the exact form the buyer will receive

cons.claim: A full read per plan per edition per state is slow unbilled work that has to be repeated on every form change
cons.example: a provider refreshing three plan tiers across two states forces six documents back through the process

cons.claim: Reading is not understanding, and a careful reader can still miss how two clauses interact
cons.example: an exclusion in one section quietly narrowed by a definition twenty pages earlier

failure_modes: building a talk track from the provider training deck rather than the contract
reading last year edition and assuming the current one matches
skipping the conditions block because it looks procedural
treating a plan name as the product identity rather than the form and edition
acceptance_tests: a marked-up copy exists for every plan and edition currently being sold, each stamped with its form identifier and state
the one-page summary reproduces the contract qualifiers rather than smoothing them
every definition that redefines an ordinary word is flagged in the working copy
revisit_triggers: the provider issues a new form, edition or state variant
a claim outcome reveals a clause interaction the read did not catch
the operator adds a plan family to the portfolio

base.update_signal: a new contract edition or state form, or a claim outcome that exposes a clause the read misunderstood

nodes.definition: Turn the covered-items schedule into a component-level map, because coverage lives at the component line and never at the appliance name. Under air conditioning the map records which parts of the unit are listed, whether the outdoor condensing unit and the indoor coil are both included, how refrigerant recovery and recharge are treated, and whether the line set, the ductwork and the thermostat are in or out. Under plumbing it records whether stoppages are covered only through an accessible cleanout, how the water heater tank is treated against its ancillary parts, and where the covered line stops at the property boundary. Under kitchen it records whether a refrigerator ice maker, its interior components and a built-in unit specialty parts are listed. The map also captures the replacement standard - whether the obligor may repair or replace at its option, and whether replacement is to comparable capacity and efficiency rather than to the same brand or model. Built once per plan edition and reused in every conversation, the map turns is my X covered from a guess into a lookup with the conditions attached to it.

included: per-item component lists including the parts silently omitted
the repair-or-replace option and the comparable-capacity replacement standard
reusable lookup structure per plan edition
excluded: the exclusion families, which are mapped separately
the dollar limits attached to each item, which are mapped separately
diagnosing whether a specific part on a specific unit has failed

pros.claim: A component map makes the common question answerable precisely instead of optimistically
pros.example: answering that the condensing unit and coil are listed while the duct run is not, rather than saying the air conditioner is covered

pros.claim: It exposes the gaps that matter for a specific home before a proposal is built
pros.example: noticing that the plan lists a standard refrigerator but not the specialty components of the built-in unit the client actually owns

cons.claim: The map is only as good as the edition it was built from and quietly goes stale
cons.example: a component quietly moved from covered to optional in a new form while the old map is still in use

cons.claim: Component granularity can overwhelm a buyer who wanted a simple answer
cons.example: a prospect who stops listening once the plumbing item is broken into six component lines

failure_modes: mapping at appliance level and inheriting all the ambiguity the contract left
assuming a component is covered because it is physically part of a listed unit
reusing a map across plan editions or across states
omitting the replacement standard so the buyer expects a like-for-like new unit
acceptance_tests: each covered item in the map lists both included components and the notable components not included
the map records the repair-or-replace option and the replacement standard in the contract own terms
the map cites the section of the current edition that each line came from
revisit_triggers: a new contract edition or optional-coverage change
a coverage question arrives that the map cannot answer
a claim outcome shows a component was treated differently than the map records

base.update_signal: a contract edition change, or a coverage question or claim outcome the current map answers wrongly

nodes.definition: Organize the exclusions section into the families that recur across this product class and, for each, state the mechanism by which it will actually be applied when a technician is standing in front of a broken unit: conditions that pre-existed coverage; improper prior installation, modification or repair; missing or improper maintenance; work needed only to satisfy code, permits or to bring a system up to current standard; cosmetic defects and parts that still perform; secondary or consequential damage, meaning the water-damaged floor rather than the failed valve; ancillary items excluded by definition such as ductwork, drain lines beyond an accessible cleanout, haul-away and disposal, cranes or roof access; hazardous-material handling; anything still covered by a manufacturer warranty, a recall or another contract; commercial or rental use of a home plan; and acts of nature. For each family the seller can say what evidence the diagnosis would rest on, what the homeowner could check before buying, and which families this particular home is most exposed to. Exclusions are taught as decision rules a buyer can apply to their own house, never recited as a list.

included: the recurring exclusion families and the evidence mechanism behind each
which families a given home is most exposed to
what a buyer can check before purchase to predict exposure
excluded: arguing or appealing an applied exclusion after a denial, which belongs to the claims-experience knowledge base
the dollar limits, which are a separate mechanism
technical judgement about whether a specific failure was caused by poor maintenance

pros.claim: Grouping exclusions into families makes them learnable and lets a buyer apply them to their own home
pros.example: a homeowner who understands the secondary-damage family immediately grasps why the failed supply line may be covered while the ruined flooring is not

pros.claim: Stating the evidence mechanism turns an abstract clause into something the buyer can act on before buying
pros.example: explaining that a prior unpermitted repair is visible to a technician prompts the client to check what the previous owner did to the furnace

cons.claim: Presented badly, the families read as a wall of reasons the plan will not pay, and the sale ends there
cons.example: a prospect who hears eleven exclusion families in a row concludes the product never pays anything

cons.claim: Family-level teaching can blur a specific contract narrower or broader wording
cons.example: treating one plan generous refrigerant handling as typical when the plan being sold excludes it

failure_modes: reading the exclusions section aloud instead of teaching the mechanisms
surfacing only the families unlikely to matter for this home
generalizing from a plan the seller used to sell to the one they are selling now
describing an exclusion as rarely enforced
acceptance_tests: every family in the current contract is represented in the taxonomy with its evidence mechanism
the seller can name the two or three families most likely to bite on this specific home
the buyer can restate at least the family that most affects their own systems
revisit_triggers: a new contract edition adds, removes or rewords an exclusion
denials in the book cluster on a family the taxonomy underweights
a new plan family with different exclusion wording enters the portfolio

base.update_signal: a reworded exclusion in a new edition, or a cluster of denials in the book resting on a family the taxonomy treats as minor

nodes.definition: Work out what the money in this contract actually does. Limits come in several shapes at once - per covered item per term, per system or trade, an aggregate across the whole term, and sub-limits on specific components or on categories like refrigerant, code compliance, permits, access or disposal - and the buying decision turns entirely on how each compares to what the repair really costs in this local market. The mechanism to teach is a comparison, not a number: take the client most expensive realistic failure, name the components involved, put the contract applicable limit beside the replacement cost range the client own local contractor would quote, and let the client see the residual they would pay themselves. Add the per-visit fee, payable on each dispatch whether or not covered work results, and sometimes again when a second trade is sent. Add the cash-in-lieu mechanism, under which the obligor may settle at what the work would cost through its own network rather than at retail. Every number in this exercise is read off this contract or sourced from the client own quotes; none is quoted from memory or from another plan.

included: the shapes limits take and how they stack on one repair
the comparison method that places a contract limit beside a locally sourced cost range
the per-visit fee and the cash-in-lieu settlement mechanism
excluded: quoting any specific cap, fee or repair cost as a fact
how the provider sets limits when designing the plan, which belongs to the products knowledge base
negotiating a settlement amount at claim time

pros.claim: Placing the limit beside a real local quote turns an abstract cap into the number the client will actually feel
pros.example: a client comparing the contract system limit with two quotes for replacing their own furnace sees the residual before they buy rather than after a denial-adjacent surprise

pros.claim: Surfacing the per-visit fee and cash-in-lieu mechanisms removes the two most common post-sale surprises about money
pros.example: a homeowner who knew a second trade means a second fee treats the second invoice as expected

cons.claim: Honest cost comparison often shows the plan covering a modest share of a large failure, which weakens the pitch
cons.example: a specialty system whose replacement cost sits far above the contract item limit

cons.claim: Sourcing genuine local cost ranges is work the seller cannot fake and cannot reuse across markets
cons.example: asking a client to get their own quote adds days to a sale cycle that a headline price would have closed

failure_modes: quoting a typical repair cost from memory or from provider marketing
explaining a per-item limit while ignoring the aggregate that sits above it
presenting the plan price without the per-visit fee alongside it
letting the client assume replacement means a new unit chosen by them
acceptance_tests: the file shows at least one limit-versus-local-cost comparison built on the client own most expensive realistic failure
no figure presented to the client lacks a source, either the contract itself or a quote the client obtained
the per-visit fee and the aggregate limit are both stated in the same conversation as the plan price
revisit_triggers: the contract edition changes a limit, a sub-limit or the fee
local repair costs move enough that a prior comparison misleads
a client reports a settlement far below the cost they were quoted locally

base.update_signal: a limit or fee change in a new edition, or client-reported settlements that sit well below locally quoted replacement cost

nodes.definition: Establish exactly when this contract begins to protect anything, using the contract own stated waiting period and effective-date rules rather than a remembered number or a competitor practice. Direct-to-homeowner sales generally start coverage only after a waiting interval running from purchase or first payment; contracts placed in connection with a real-estate transaction commonly attach at or after closing and treat the waiting interval differently, and that difference is a contract term rather than a favour anyone can grant. What the buyer must leave knowing: the calendar date on which a claim first becomes possible, that a failure occurring or discovered before that date will generally be handled under the pre-existing and no-coverage provisions, what happens if the closing slips or the contract is issued late, and how occupancy or a vacant period affects the start. The claim filed inside the waiting window is the most common early complaint in this product class and the easiest to eliminate: write the start date and the waiting-period end date on the summary the buyer takes away.

included: deriving effective date and waiting-period end from the contract
the real-estate-transaction variant treated as a contract term
what a slipped closing, late issuance or vacancy does to the start date
excluded: any promise to accelerate coverage or to have a claim considered early
channel mechanics of placing a plan into a closing, which belong to the distribution knowledge base
handling a claim that was filed inside the window, which belongs to the claims-experience knowledge base

pros.claim: A written start date and waiting-period end date removes the single most common early dispute
pros.example: a buyer whose dryer fails in week two consults the date on their summary rather than calling to accuse the seller

pros.claim: It also filters out the purchase that was really an attempt to buy a repair
pros.example: a caller with a currently leaking water heater hears the start date and self-selects out before paying

cons.claim: The start date is exactly what an urgent buyer does not want to hear, and stating it loses that sale
cons.example: a homeowner with a struggling furnace in a cold snap ends the call once the waiting interval is explained

cons.claim: Dates depend on events the seller does not control, so the answer often has to stay conditional
cons.example: a contract tied to a closing whose date moves twice before it funds

failure_modes: quoting a waiting period length from memory or from a different plan
implying that a friendly administrator will overlook an early claim
leaving the date verbal so nothing exists to point at later
failing to revisit the date when the closing moves
acceptance_tests: the summary the buyer takes away carries the coverage start date and the waiting-period end date in writing
the dates are traceable to the contract clause rather than to a remembered norm
where the start depends on a closing, the file records how the date will be confirmed once the closing funds
revisit_triggers: a closing date moves or the contract is issued later than expected
the contract edition changes the waiting-period or effective-date rule
an early claim is refused for timing on a file where the date was never written down

base.update_signal: an edition change to the effective-date or waiting-period clause, or an early-claim refusal on a file where the dates were not documented

nodes.definition: The pre-existing-condition clause is best taught as an evidence test, because that is exactly how it gets applied: the obligor asks whether the failure existed before coverage began, and whether it was either known to the buyer or would have been detectable by visual inspection or simple mechanical test at that time. Both halves matter. Unknown does not rescue a condition that a walkthrough or a routine test would have revealed, and a home inspection report cuts both ways - it can establish that a system was sound, and it can establish that a defect was documented and therefore known. The seller job is to explain the test before the sale, ask directly what is currently not working or has been repeatedly repaired, and treat an answer like it has been making a noise for months as a stop sign for that item rather than an opening. Where a system is already failing, the honest positions are to buy for the rest of the home while understanding that item is unlikely to pay, or not to buy. The clause is never described as a formality, and the seller never coaches a client on how to phrase a condition.

included: the known-or-detectable two-part test and how each half is evidenced
how an inspection report can help or hurt the buyer
the seller response when a client describes a currently failing system
excluded: advising a client how to describe a condition to improve a claim outcome, which is never acceptable
determining whether a specific failure predates coverage, which is the obligor call at claim time
the maintenance-history family, which is a separate mechanism

pros.claim: Teaching the clause as an evidence test lets a buyer predict their own outcome instead of hoping
pros.example: a client who knows a documented inspection defect is discoverable stops expecting the plan to fund that repair

pros.claim: It surfaces the deals that should not happen while they can still be redirected
pros.example: a caller who mentions a furnace that keeps shutting off is steered to a repair quote and a later purchase rather than into a doomed claim

cons.claim: The clause is broad enough that an honest explanation makes the product sound weaker than a competitor pitch that skips it
cons.example: a rival seller who never mentions detectability wins the sale the honest explanation lost

cons.claim: It puts the seller in the uncomfortable position of asking questions whose answers can kill the sale
cons.example: asking what is currently not working and getting an answer that ends the conversation

failure_modes: presenting the clause as boilerplate that rarely matters
hearing about a failing unit and selling anyway without recording it
hinting at what a client should or should not mention
treating unknown as sufficient protection for the buyer
acceptance_tests: the buyer can restate that both known and reasonably detectable conditions fall outside coverage
any client-described current failure appears in the intake record with the date it was described
no note, script or recording contains coaching about how to characterize a condition
revisit_triggers: the clause wording changes in a new edition
a denial in the book turns on detectability in a way the explanation did not anticipate
an inspection report surfaces after the sale that contradicts the intake

base.update_signal: an edition rewording of the pre-existing clause, or a denial that applies detectability more broadly than the explanation assumed

nodes.definition: A large share of refusals in this product class turn not on whether a part is listed but on whether the failure is attributed to missing or improper maintenance, and in practice the homeowner is the one who has to show otherwise. The competent seller explains this before the sale and hands the buyer a habit rather than a warning: keep dated invoices for annual heating and cooling service, keep filter-change and water-heater flush records, keep the paperwork from any prior repair including who performed it and what was replaced, and photograph the model and serial plates of the major units at the start of the term so the equipment can be identified later without argument. This costs the client almost nothing, materially improves their position when a technician writes lack of maintenance on a diagnosis, and protects the seller too, because the file shows the client was told. It also feeds the buying decision: a home with no service history at all is a home where this family of refusals is more likely to bite, which belongs in the tier conversation rather than being discovered at the first claim.

included: the maintenance-attribution refusal mechanism explained before purchase
the concrete record-keeping habit handed to the buyer
using absent service history as an input to the tier and decline decisions
excluded: performing or arranging the maintenance itself
disputing a maintenance-based refusal after the fact, which belongs to the claims-experience knowledge base
judging whether a given maintenance interval was technically adequate

pros.claim: A record habit started at sale exists before it is needed, which is the only time it can be created honestly
pros.example: a buyer who kept two years of dated service invoices can answer a lack-of-maintenance diagnosis with paperwork rather than recollection

pros.claim: It gives the seller something genuinely useful to hand over that costs nothing and is remembered
pros.example: a simple receipts folder and a photograph of each nameplate handed over with the contract

cons.claim: Most buyers will not keep the records regardless of how clearly the habit is explained
cons.example: a homeowner who agrees enthusiastically at sale and has nothing filed when a claim arrives eighteen months later

cons.claim: Explaining the burden reveals that coverage is conditional on the buyer own diligence, which dampens the appeal
cons.example: a prospect who concludes that the plan only pays if they also pay for annual servicing

failure_modes: mentioning maintenance as a footnote rather than as a refusal mechanism
implying that records guarantee approval
skipping the nameplate photographs so the covered equipment is later hard to identify
ignoring the absence of any service history when recommending a tier
acceptance_tests: the closing packet contains the record habit in writing, naming the specific documents to keep
the file notes whether any service history exists for the major systems
the buyer can restate that a maintenance-attributed failure is a common refusal path
revisit_triggers: a maintenance-attributed refusal reaches a client who followed the habit
the contract edition changes its maintenance requirements
the provider begins requiring documentation the habit does not produce

base.update_signal: a refusal attributed to maintenance on a client who did keep records, or a contract change to the maintenance requirement

nodes.definition: Build a factual profile of the actual house that determines whether a contract can plausibly pay for itself, using observable inputs rather than fear. Read the age and type of each major system off its nameplate, note whether units appear original to the construction, look for evidence of prior replacement or repair, account for local stress factors such as water hardness on heaters and coils or heavy seasonal load on cooling equipment, count the covered appliances that actually exist in the home rather than the ones the plan lists, and mark specialty or high-end equipment whose parts cost sits well above ordinary against the contract limits. Two inputs are as important as any hardware fact: the homeowner own repair capability, and whether they have cash available for an unplanned failure. The profile is expressed in bands and mechanisms - a water heater at the older end of typical service life in a hard-water area, a built-in refrigerator whose specialty parts price above the item limit - never as an invented failure probability or a predicted repair bill. This is where the vertical central temptation lives: the same facts can be delivered as a mechanism or as a scare, and only the first is legitimate.

included: observable system inventory, age bands and local stress factors
the homeowner repair capability and cash-buffer inputs
expressing risk as bands and mechanisms rather than as numbers
excluded: any predicted failure probability, expected repair cost or savings projection
technical inspection or diagnosis of equipment condition
recommending a specific plan, which is the tier-fit decision

pros.claim: A factual profile makes the recommendation defensible and repeatable rather than a matter of persuasion
pros.example: recommending against an upgrade because the home has neither a pool nor a second refrigerator, stated from the inventory rather than from instinct

pros.claim: Including the cash-buffer question routinely surfaces the buyers for whom self-funding is simply better
pros.example: a client with ample reserves and newer systems who leaves with a repair-fund plan instead of a contract

cons.claim: The inputs are self-reported and visual, so the profile carries real uncertainty
cons.example: a nameplate that is unreadable and an owner who does not know when the unit was replaced

cons.claim: The same profile can be weaponized into fear, and the line is a matter of delivery rather than content
cons.example: presenting an ageing water heater as a fact about service-life bands, or as a countdown to a flooded garage

failure_modes: converting age observations into predictions of imminent failure
counting plan-listed appliances the home does not have
skipping the cash-buffer question because it invites a no-sale
recording opinions about condition as though they were inspection findings
acceptance_tests: the profile lists each major system with its observable age band and its source, such as a nameplate photograph
no element of the profile states a failure probability or a predicted repair cost
the homeowner repair capability and cash-buffer answers are recorded
revisit_triggers: an inspection or a technician visit contradicts the recorded system ages
the client replaces or repairs a major system mid-conversation
the plan portfolio changes which equipment classes matter

base.update_signal: an inspection report or technician finding that contradicts the recorded system inventory or ages

nodes.definition: Choose the tier and the optional coverages by testing each increment against the profile with three questions: does the higher tier add components this home actually has, does it raise the limit that would bind on this home most expensive realistic failure, and does it remove an exclusion that would otherwise apply here. If the answer to all three is no, the upgrade is priced convenience rather than protection and should be declined out loud. Optional coverages - pool and spa equipment, well pump, septic system, second refrigerator, guest quarters, roof-leak riders - are worth their price only when the asset exists, is the owner responsibility rather than an association responsibility, and is not already excluded on another ground such as commercial use or prior improper installation. The reasoning is stated to the client in those terms, including the uncomfortable version: this tier costs more and does not change the limit that would bind on your furnace, so I do not recommend it. Where the plan family pays the seller more for the tier that fits the home worse, the conflict resolves toward the client and the reasoning goes in the file.

included: the three-question upgrade test applied to each tier and rider
the asset-exists and owner-responsibility test for optional coverages
stating the recommendation and its reasoning where compensation and fit disagree
excluded: how tiers are constructed and compensated by the provider, which belongs to the products knowledge base
the decision not to sell at all, which is a separate path
renewal-time tier changes, which belong to the renewals knowledge base

pros.claim: The three-question test makes upgrade recommendations checkable by anyone reading the file
pros.example: a rider declined in writing because the home has no well and the pump line therefore covers nothing

pros.claim: Declining an upgrade that does not move the binding limit buys credibility that carries the rest of the recommendation
pros.example: a client who hears one tier talked down accepts the recommendation on the tier that fits

cons.claim: The test systematically reduces the revenue per sale where compensation rises with tier
cons.example: recommending the base plan on a home whose only meaningful exposure is a single ageing system

cons.claim: Fit judgements rest on a profile built from imperfect observation
cons.example: recommending against an appliance rider because a unit looked recently replaced when it was not

failure_modes: selling the tier by category name without checking the home has the equipment
adding riders for assets the association or landlord is responsible for
upgrading when the binding constraint is the limit rather than the component list
leaving the reasoning verbal so the recommendation cannot be reconstructed
acceptance_tests: each recommended or declined increment carries a written answer to the three-question test
every optional coverage recommended corresponds to an asset confirmed present and in the owner responsibility
the file records any case where the fitting recommendation paid the seller less
revisit_triggers: the client adds or removes major equipment such as a pool or a second refrigerator
the provider restructures tiers, riders or their limits
a claim outcome shows a recommended rider did not cover what the client expected

base.update_signal: a provider tier or rider restructure, or a claim outcome showing a recommended rider did not cover the exposure it was chosen for

nodes.definition: A defined path that ends in the sentence you should not buy this, treated as a normal outcome of competent work rather than a failure of it. It fires when the home systems are new and still inside manufacturer warranty, when the client reserves make paying for a repair outright plainly cheaper than the stack of contract price plus per-visit fees plus the residual above the limits, when the specific failures the client is worried about sit inside exclusion families that will not pay for them, when the limits sit far below the local replacement cost of the specialty equipment the client actually cares about, when the client cannot accept that the obligor rather than the seller decides claims, and when a vulnerable buyer cannot follow the terms after a genuine attempt. The path produces an artifact rather than an awkward silence: a short written note of why the plan is not recommended and what to do instead - build a repair reserve, take the manufacturer extended coverage on the one unit that matters, revisit when the systems age. A declined sale protects the referral stream and the renewal book far more than the lost commission costs, and it is the clearest evidence that the disclosure conversation was real.

included: the trigger conditions for recommending no purchase
the written no-sale note and the alternatives offered
keeping the relationship open for a later, better-fitting purchase
excluded: advising a client to cancel or not renew an existing plan, which belongs to the renewals knowledge base
personalized financial advice about how to fund repairs
disparaging a competitor product to justify the decline

pros.claim: A no-sale note converts a lost commission into a durable referral source
pros.example: a homeowner told their year-old systems do not need a plan comes back two years later and sends a neighbour in the meantime

pros.claim: It removes the sales most likely to end in a refusal, a chargeback or a public complaint
pros.example: declining to sell to a caller whose only concern is a system already failing

cons.claim: The path costs immediate revenue and is invisible in any pipeline metric that counts closes
cons.example: a seller whose honest declines make their conversion rate look worse than a colleague who sells everyone

cons.claim: A decline can be wrong, since new equipment fails too and reserves get spent
cons.example: a client advised to self-fund who then faces two failures in one season

failure_modes: downgrading to a cheap tier to salvage a sale that should not happen
declining silently by going quiet rather than saying it plainly
framing the decline as the client fault for having old equipment
leaving no record that the recommendation was made
acceptance_tests: every decline leaves a dated written note of the reason and the alternative suggested
no file shows a downgrade substituted for a decline where a trigger condition was met
the client received the note rather than only hearing it
revisit_triggers: the client circumstances change, such as systems ageing past warranty or reserves being spent
the provider adds a plan whose structure fits a previously declined profile
a declined client returns with a new home or a new concern

base.update_signal: declined clients returning with changed circumstances, or a new plan structure that fits a profile previously declined

nodes.definition: Before the sale closes, narrate the claim experience the buyer will actually have, because the distance between the imagined experience and the real one is where this product class earns its reputation. The preview covers only what the contract and the administrator process actually state: how a claim is opened and within what time of discovering a failure, that the administrator assigns a contractor from its network rather than the homeowner picking their own plumber, what the contract says about using an outside contractor and what pre-authorization it requires, that a per-visit fee is due on each dispatch, that the technician diagnosis is the evidence the obligor decides on, that repair or replace is generally the obligor option and to what standard, that non-covered charges may be quoted alongside covered work and paid directly by the homeowner, and that timelines depend on parts availability and contractor scheduling rather than on the seller. The preview is delivered face to face or on the call, referenced to contract sections, and stops firmly short of promising response times or service levels the document does not state.

included: the mechanics of opening a claim and who assigns the contractor
fees, diagnosis-as-evidence, repair-or-replace option and non-covered charges
the refusal to promise response times the contract does not state
excluded: guiding the client through a live claim or a refusal, which belongs to the claims-experience knowledge base
any service-level or response-time promise
the administrator internal contractor-network operations

pros.claim: A preview delivered at sale is the cheapest reputation insurance in the business
pros.example: a homeowner who was told the administrator picks the contractor does not experience that as a bait and switch at the first claim

pros.claim: It reframes the seller as the person who told the truth first, which is what survives a difficult claim
pros.example: a client whose repair took two weeks for parts remembers being told timelines depend on availability

cons.claim: Describing the process honestly makes the product sound less convenient than the marketing did
cons.example: a prospect who wanted their own trusted plumber hears that the network assigns one and hesitates

cons.claim: The preview describes an experience the seller does not control and cannot guarantee
cons.example: an administrator whose actual dispatch performance is worse than the process description implies

failure_modes: promising a response time or a service level the contract does not state
skipping the contractor-assignment point because it dampens enthusiasm
omitting that non-covered charges can appear on a covered job
delivering the preview after payment as part of a welcome message
acceptance_tests: the buyer can restate who assigns the contractor and what they will pay per visit
no preview statement asserts a response time or service level absent from the contract
the preview is documented as delivered before payment
revisit_triggers: the administrator changes the claim intake or contractor-assignment process
clients report an experience materially different from the preview
the contract edition changes pre-authorization or outside-contractor rules

base.update_signal: a change in the administrator claim process, or client-reported experiences that diverge from the preview

nodes.definition: Rendering contract language into ordinary speech is the core teaching skill of this subdomain, and it has one hard rule: a translation may simplify the sentence but may never widen the promise. In practice that means showing the clause and reading it before paraphrasing; keeping the contract qualifiers alive in the paraphrase, because subject to, up to, at the obligor option, accessible and normal wear and tear are the clause rather than decoration; never swapping a conditional for an unconditional, so that component is listed, subject to these conditions and this limit does not become that is covered; checking understanding by asking the buyer to restate the limit in their own words rather than asking whether it makes sense; and preferring to show the page over summarizing it, especially for exclusions, limits and the waiting period. Where the buyer language is not the contract language, use the provider translated materials if they exist and bring in a professional interpreter or a trusted family member rather than improvising a translation the seller cannot verify, and note in the file how the language gap was handled.

included: the rule that simplification may not widen a promise
preserving contract qualifiers and using restatement to check understanding
handling a language gap with translated materials or an interpreter
excluded: legal interpretation of an ambiguous clause, which escalates to the provider or counsel
rewriting or restating contract terms in any document that purports to be the contract
the decision about which plan to recommend

pros.claim: Restatement testing catches the misunderstanding that a yes-I-follow never reveals
pros.example: a buyer who says the plan replaces the whole unit is corrected before signing rather than at the first claim

pros.claim: Showing the page rather than summarizing it makes the document, not the seller, the source of the promise
pros.example: pointing at the exclusion paragraph so the buyer reads the word accessible for themselves

cons.claim: Faithful paraphrase is slower and clumsier than the confident simple sentence a buyer prefers
cons.example: the accurate answer about a listed component subject to conditions and a limit, next to a competitor flat yes

cons.claim: Keeping every qualifier can obscure the practical answer the client needs
cons.example: a translation so hedged that the client cannot tell whether their water heater is generally in or out

failure_modes: dropping qualifiers to make a sentence land better
confirming understanding with a yes-or-no question instead of a restatement
improvising a second-language explanation the seller cannot verify
handing over a seller-written summary that reads as though it were the contract
acceptance_tests: every paraphrase used in the sale preserves the contract qualifiers for that clause
understanding is verified by buyer restatement on at least the limits, exclusions and waiting period
any seller-written summary is labelled as a summary and points to the governing sections
revisit_triggers: a buyer restatement reveals a systematic misunderstanding of a specific clause
the contract edition rewords a clause the talk track paraphrases
the operator begins selling to a language community without provider translated materials

base.update_signal: buyer restatements that repeatedly misread the same clause, or an edition rewording a clause the talk track paraphrases

nodes.definition: A repeatable answer form for the question that dominates every conversation in this business. The honest structure has three parts: what the document lists or omits for that component, the conditions attached to it such as the waiting period, the pre-existing test, the maintenance requirement and the applicable limit, and who decides at claim time. Spoken, it sounds like this: your dishwasher is a listed item and its control board is included, subject to the item limit and the pre-existing condition test, and whether a particular failure is covered is the obligor determination once a technician has diagnosed it. When the component map cannot resolve the question - an unusual system, an ambiguity in a definition, an edge of the covered-items schedule - the answer is that the seller does not know and will get it answered in writing, followed by an actual written question to the provider and a written answer back to the client. Every material coverage question and its answer is logged with a date, because these are precisely the sentences that get disputed later, and a logged answer protects the buyer as much as the seller.

included: the three-part answer form ending in who decides
the escalation path for questions the map cannot resolve
logging material questions and answers with dates
excluded: predicting how the obligor will decide a specific future claim
answering questions about an already-filed claim, which belongs to the claims-experience knowledge base
any commitment made on the provider behalf without written confirmation

pros.claim: A fixed answer form makes accuracy a habit rather than a matter of the seller mood or the prospect pressure
pros.example: the same three-part structure used on the fifth question of a long call, when improvisation is most tempting

pros.claim: Written escalation converts the seller uncertainty into a durable answer the client can rely on
pros.example: an unusual heating system question answered in writing by the provider and forwarded to the client

cons.claim: The form is slower and less satisfying than a direct yes, and prospects notice
cons.example: a buyer who wanted a one-word answer and heard three clauses instead

cons.claim: Escalation depends on a provider that answers in writing and in reasonable time
cons.example: a question sent for written confirmation that is still unanswered when the buyer needs to decide

failure_modes: answering yes when the honest answer is listed subject to conditions
guessing at the edge of the covered-items schedule instead of escalating
escalating verbally and relaying an unwritten answer as though it were confirmed
leaving the question and answer unlogged
acceptance_tests: material coverage questions in the file each carry a dated answer in the three-part form
no answer in the file guarantees a claim outcome
every escalated question has a written provider answer attached before it is relayed
revisit_triggers: a question recurs often enough that the component map should answer it
a provider written answer contradicts an answer previously given
a claim outcome contradicts a logged answer

base.update_signal: a provider written answer or claim outcome that contradicts an answer previously logged in the file

nodes.definition: Compare plans on the axes that actually decide outcomes rather than on the headline price: which components are listed, how broad each exclusion family is, the shape and size of the limits, the per-visit fee, the waiting period, the cancellation and refund method, and who the obligor is. Laid out side by side on those axes, a cheaper plan usually reveals itself as a narrower one, and choosing narrower with open eyes is a legitimate decision a buyer is entitled to make. The second half of this unit is a prohibition with no exceptions: no catastrophe storytelling, no invented failure statistics, no repair-cost figures the seller cannot source, no claims that a specific unit is about to fail, no manufactured urgency about a price that will disappear, and no disparaging characterization of a competitor obligor that the seller cannot support from that competitor own document. Where a number would help and cannot be sourced, it is described as a mechanism and left unquantified. Fear closes a sale once; a normalized comparison closes it in a way that survives the first claim.

included: the normalized comparison axes across competing plans
the prohibition on fear framing, unsourced figures and manufactured urgency
sourcing any comparison figure from the contract or the client own quotes
excluded: competitive positioning and channel-level marketing strategy, which belong to the distribution knowledge base
characterizing a competitor obligor claims behaviour without documentary support
renewal-time comparison against the incumbent plan, which belongs to the renewals knowledge base

pros.claim: A normalized comparison lets a buyer see why a cheaper plan is cheaper, which is the only fair way to lose or win on price
pros.example: two plans laid beside each other showing that the lower price omits the coil and caps the system lower

pros.claim: Refusing fear framing keeps the seller inside the ethical line that most complaints in this vertical cross
pros.example: declining to tell an anxious homeowner their compressor is on borrowed time to close a same-day sale

cons.claim: Fear and urgency demonstrably close sales faster, so the rule has a visible cost and an invisible benefit
cons.example: a competitor using a catastrophe story wins the prospect who left the honest comparison to think

cons.claim: Building a fair comparison requires the competitor actual document, which is often unavailable
cons.example: a prospect who has only a marketing page for the rival plan and no contract to compare

failure_modes: comparing on price and covered-item names alone
quoting failure statistics or repair costs the seller cannot source
implying a competitor denies claims without documentary support
introducing a deadline that does not exist to force a decision
acceptance_tests: every comparison presented covers components, exclusions, limits, fee, waiting period and obligor
every figure used carries a source, either a contract or a client-obtained quote
no sales material or recorded call contains catastrophe framing or an invented deadline
revisit_triggers: a competitor changes its contract in a way the comparison misrepresents
a prospect reports being told something the comparison should have addressed
the operator adds a plan family whose axes differ

base.update_signal: a competitor contract change that makes the comparison inaccurate, or a complaint that a sales conversation used fear or urgency framing

nodes.definition: The buyer receives the real document before purchase - the full contract, or the provider sample of the exact form and edition that will be issued for their state and plan - not a brochure, not a comparison chart and not a summary the seller wrote. The operational work is version control: knowing which edition applies to this sale, confirming that the copy delivered matches what the provider will actually issue, recording the delivery date and the channel it went through, and re-checking the edition whenever the provider updates forms, adds a state or launches a plan family. In channels that compress the timeline, the document still goes first and the walkthrough is scheduled around it rather than the reverse. This is the cheapest protection either side gets: a buyer holding the actual contract before deciding cannot credibly be told later that they were shown something else, and the seller file shows precisely which document was delivered and when. Where a provider will not supply a pre-sale sample of the applicable form, that itself is a finding worth escalating rather than working around.

included: pre-purchase delivery of the exact form and edition
edition version control and delivery-date recording
escalating a provider that cannot supply the applicable pre-sale sample
excluded: whether a given jurisdiction mandates pre-sale delivery, which is an obligation class to verify
the walkthrough of the document, which is the disclosure conversation
storage and security of delivered documents

pros.claim: Delivering the governing document before the decision ends most disputes about what the buyer was shown
pros.example: a dated delivery record of the exact state form beside the buyer later recollection of a brochure

pros.claim: Version control catches the quiet form change that would otherwise turn a correct talk track into a misstatement
pros.example: noticing that a new edition moved a component into an optional coverage before the next sale is made

cons.claim: Handing over a long contract before the conversation loses some prospects at the sight of it
cons.example: a buyer who reads the exclusions section alone and stops returning calls

cons.claim: Version control is administrative overhead that grows with every state and plan family added
cons.example: an operator tracking several forms across two states and three tiers

failure_modes: sending a marketing brochure and calling it the contract
delivering last edition sample because it is the one on file
delivering after payment and backdating the disclosure narrative
delivering the wrong state form for the property
acceptance_tests: every sale file records the edition delivered, the delivery date and the channel
the delivered document matches the form the provider issued, checked after issuance
no file shows a delivery date later than the payment date
revisit_triggers: the provider publishes a new form, edition or state variant
an issued contract differs from the sample that was delivered
the operator begins selling in an additional state
